solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Love story involving fine group as a possible compensation

parts.note: love is nil in tennis, the letter O

indicators.note: a story involving something holds it within, so the story's letters go round the others

parts.note: a fable is a story
F is the abbreviation for fine on pencil grades
a set is a group

explanation.surface: A romance novelist tries to pay off a fine and their band's debts with a love story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involving' puts F and SET inside the story, giving FFSETABLE; O for love (tennis nil) goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Something offsetable can be set against a loss, so it serves as a possible counterbalancing compensation.

clue.text: Soften by kneading, careless when following mum

indicators.note: following places the careless word after the word for mum

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother
lax means careless or slack

explanation.surface: A baker kneads dough loosely, imitating mother's slapdash technique.
explanation.definitionFit: Malax is a rare verb meaning to make supple by working or massaging, like malaxate.

clue.text: Girl with pullover should keep mom's toddler happy

parts.note: baby is slang for a girl or sweetheart
a jumper is a British word for a pullover sweater

explanation.surface: A girl in a pullover is babysitting an American mother's small child.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is the British word for a knitted pullover; 'mom' signals the device is American.
explanation.definitionFit: A baby jumper is a harness on a spring in which an infant can bounce, an amusement for toddlers.

clue.text: Old convict: one with time doubled isn't common

parts.note: a means one
T is the abbreviation for time, written twice
ain't is the common or vulgar form of isn't

explanation.surface: A former prisoner who served double time is unusual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old convict' is a verb here, not a former prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: Attaint is an archaic verb meaning to convict or condemn someone, especially of treason.

clue.text: Snack bar's opening: cut piece from the press?

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of bar

indicators.note: cut means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: an item is a newspaper piece

explanation.surface: At a snack bar's launch, a slice of a newspaper article is trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: A bite is a light meal or snack, as in grabbing a bite to eat.

clue.text: Sweet wine Jock's beloved imbibes before pork

indicators.note: imbibes means takes in, so the sweetheart's letters hold the rest

parts.note: jo is a Scots word for a sweetheart; Jock stands for a Scot
ere is a poetic word for before
a pig is the animal pork comes from

explanation.surface: A Scotsman's girlfriend drinks a dessert wine before her pork course.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerepigo is a heavy, sweet fortified wine, originally Portuguese, now made in South Africa.

clue.text: Clear passage through part of runs to pasture

indicators.note: part of says the letters lie within the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run in the middle of letters 2-7 of 'runs to pasture'

explanation.surface: A path is cleared for livestock to run out to the field.
explanation.definitionFit: To unstop is to remove a blockage so that something can flow through freely.

clue.text: Versatile jazzman? He makes money, certainly

parts.note: M stands for money, as in the money supply measures M1 and M3
oke is a variant of OK, meaning yes, certainly

explanation.surface: A jazz musician who can play anything makes good money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He makes' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A moke, in slang, is a performer who plays several instruments, hence versatile.

clue.text: Ancient homily on saint, most apt

parts.note: prone is an obsolete word for a sermon or homily

explanation.surface: An old sermon about a saint was particularly fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Prone can mean inclined or liable, so the superlative is most inclined, i.e. most apt to do something.

clue.text: Our diet needs adapting to become frivolous, à la française

indicators.note: something that needs adapting must be rearranged into a new form

explanation.surface: We must change our eating habits if we want to become light-hearted, French-style.
explanation.definitionFit: Étourdi is French for thoughtless or giddy, used in English for a scatterbrained, flighty person.

clue.text: Rubber substitute causing uncontrollable movement in bearing

indicators.note: in places the twitch within the word for bearing

parts.note: face can mean outward appearance or bearing
a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: A worn mechanical bearing makes something jerk wildly, so rubber is needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bearing' looks mechanical, but it means one's demeanour; 'in' puts the twitch inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Factice is a rubbery material made by vulcanising vegetable oils, used to extend natural rubber.

clue.text: Bridge player having void in hearts, capturing a third of tricks in turn

indicators.note: capturing means holding the following letters inside

parts.note: void means none, so no
H is the card-game abbreviation for hearts

indicators.note: in turn means the two letters are read backwards

parts.note: the first two of the six letters of tricks

explanation.surface: A bridge player with no hearts still wins some tricks.
explanation.definitionFit: North is one of the four compass-named seats at the bridge table, partnered with South.

clue.text: Fragments machine repairer has left inside

definitions.note: plural noun; the answer is the singular, also used as a collective

indicators.note: inside puts the left letter within the repairer

parts.note: a fitter assembles and repairs machinery

explanation.surface: A mechanic has left broken pieces inside a machine.
explanation.definitionFit: Flitters are tatters or small shreds, so a flitter is a fragment.

clue.text: The misguided need Dettol (nothing less), grasping one?

definitions.text: The misguided need Dettol (nothing less), grasping one?

indicators.note: grasping means holding the next letter inside
misguided means led astray, so the letters are rearranged
less means without, so that letter is removed

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O
a means one

explanation.surface: Fools who grab a nettle need antiseptic, unless it is the harmless kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'less' removes O (nothing) from NEED DETTOL, leaving NEEDDETTL; 'misguided' rearranges that to DEDNETTLE, and 'grasping' wraps it round A. Only a misguided person would want Dettol for this plant, since it does not sting.
explanation.definitionFit: The deadnettle is a nettle-like plant without stinging hairs, so it can be grasped safely.

clue.text: Native American chief, no more? It's a long story

indicators.note: no more says the word more is taken away

parts.note: a sagamore is a chief of some Algonquian peoples
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tale of a tribal leader who has died runs on and on.
explanation.definitionFit: A saga is a long narrative, originally a medieval Norse prose epic.

clue.text: Female prisoner, unruly teen put inside directly

indicators.note: put inside places the rearranged letters within the word for directly

parts.note: due means directly, as in due north

indicators.note: unruly means disorderly, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wild teenage girl is sent straight to jail.
explanation.definitionFit: A détenue is a woman held in custody, especially for political reasons; détenu is the masculine.

clue.text: Dig up old — front of wording missing — battered 'RIP' follows

indicators.note: follows places the rearranged letters after the shortened word
the front of a word is its first letter
missing means that letter is dropped

parts.note: text is the wording of a document

indicators.note: battered means knocked out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An old gravestone is dug up, its inscription damaged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'front of' and 'missing' leave EXT; 'battered' makes IRP, which 'follows' it. The 'old' in 'Dig up old' marks the definition as archaic, not the abbreviation EX.
explanation.definitionFit: Extirp is an obsolete form of extirpate, to root out or pull up entirely.

clue.text: Pronounces oriental soup 'bum'

parts.note: pho is a Vietnamese noodle soup
nates are the buttocks; bum is British slang for the bottom

explanation.surface: Someone declares an Asian soup to be rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: Bum is British slang for the backside, not a tramp.
explanation.definitionFit: To phonate is to produce speech sounds with the vocal cords, i.e. to utter.

clue.text: Timeless carouser, one Falstaff, say?

indicators.note: time-less means the T for time is removed

parts.note: a toper is a heavy drinker

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's Falstaff is an eternal reveller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Timeless' leaves OPER. Falstaff the drinker is a red herring: Verdi wrote an opera named after him.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi's Falstaff is an example of the genre of staged musical drama.

clue.text: Who isn't irritated by parking in conurbation?

indicators.note: irritated means stirred up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Is anyone in the city not annoyed by the parking?
explanation.definitionFit: A township is a town or urban settlement; a conurbation is a sprawling urban area.

clue.text: By the way, more than half of strong drinks make you slash

parts.note: ob. is short for obiter, Latin for by the way

parts.words: more than half of strong drinks
parts.note: the first five of the eight letters of liqueurs

explanation.surface: Incidentally, spirits make you want to cut someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slash' is the punctuation mark, not a cut or (British slang) a pee.
explanation.definitionFit: An oblique is the typographical stroke /, also called a slash or solidus.

clue.text: He stitched cap with frills

indicators.note: to frill is to gather and pleat fabric, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A man sewed a fancy cap with ruffles.
explanation.definitionFit: Whipcat is an old slang term for a tailor, someone who sews clothes.

clue.text: What could make me a lord?

definitions.text: What could make me a lord?

indicators.note: could make means the letters can be rearranged to form something else

explanation.surface: Someone wonders how to get ennobled.
explanation.definitionFit: An earldom is the rank or title of an earl, which would make a commoner a peer.

clue.text: Form of argot a semi-polyglot rubbished and binned?

indicators.note: rubbished and binned: the trashed letters are also thrown into the bin, so the bin's letters go round them

parts.note: binned gives the word bin, the place the rubbish is thrown

indicators.note: rubbished means trashed, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the second half of polyglot

explanation.surface: Someone half able in languages throws out a bad attempt at slang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rubbished' gives OGLAT, which, as the surface says, is then binned: 'and' adds the second action of putting it in a bin. Only the second half of polyglot is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Bog Latin is a secret jargon or cant, mock Latin used by vagrants.

clue.text: You require a horn or buzzer for each

parts.note: a bee is something that buzzes
per means for each

explanation.surface: Every person needs an alarm or a horn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You require a' and 'or' join the parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A beeper is a device that beeps, such as a car hooter or a pager.

clue.text: Old poet's immediately energized after book

indicators.note: after places the word for energized behind the book's letter

parts.note: live means charged with electricity

explanation.surface: An old poet suddenly comes alive once he picks up a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Blive is Spenser's form of belive, an archaic word for at once or soon.

clue.text: Sweet Rosie's cut short English in old Scottish exam (6, two words)

indicators.note: cut short means the name loses its last letter

parts.note: Sweet Rosie O'Grady is a popular 1890s song

explanation.surface: A girl's sweet surname is shortened in an English exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut short' drops the last letter of O'GRADY to leave OGRAD. The O grade was the Scottish counterpart of the O level, later replaced by the Standard Grade.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ordinary grade was a former Scottish school examination taken around sixteen.

clue.text: Cook making case for exotic bird or tropical fish

indicators.note: making a case for means enclosing, so the cook's letters go round the bird

parts.note: to do food is to cook it
the ani is a tropical American cuckoo

explanation.surface: A chef serves up a rare bird or a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A danio is a small brightly coloured carp-like aquarium fish from South Asia.

clue.text: Grasp without hearing lecturer repaid toiling

indicators.note: toiling means labouring, so the letters are worked over into a new order

explanation.surface: A deaf lecturer is paid back for his hard work.
explanation.definitionFit: To lip-read is to understand speech by watching the speaker's mouth rather than hearing.

clue.text: Indication of lung disease? MO lost confidence

indicators.note: lost means the two letters MO are taken away

parts.note: morale is confidence or spirit

explanation.surface: A doctor lost confidence about a sign of lung disease.
explanation.walkthrough: MO is Medical Officer, a military doctor; 'lost' takes those letters from MORALE.
explanation.definitionFit: A rale is a rattling sound heard in the chest, a symptom of disease of the lungs.

clue.text: Formerly straight, slewed by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it says the word is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: slewed is slang for drunk, i.e. tight

explanation.surface: Something that used to be straight now looks twisted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'straight' is short for straightaway; 'slewed' is drunk, not twisted, and 'by the sound of it' makes TIGHT a homophone.
explanation.definitionFit: Tite is an obsolete adverb meaning at once or promptly, i.e. straightaway.

clue.text: It keeps mill-wheel turning — hindrance restricts one

indicators.note: restricts means confines, so the hindrance's letters go round the next

parts.note: a let is a hindrance, as in without let or hindrance
a means one

explanation.surface: An obstacle holds back a single water mill.
explanation.definitionFit: A leat is an open channel bringing water to a mill wheel, which powers it.

clue.text: Free camping? Sort of fork provided

parts.note: camping means staying in a tent, and being in one, so the word for free goes inside a tent
to rid is to free

explanation.surface: Free camping comes with a cutlery fork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'camping' is read as 'in a tent', so it both supplies the outer word and says the inner one goes within it.
explanation.definitionFit: A trident is a three-pronged spear, a type of fork associated with Neptune.

clue.text: Property of the same value, first to last

indicators.note: first to last means the opening letter moves to the end

parts.note: equal means of the same value

explanation.surface: Two estates are valued equally, from first to last.
explanation.definitionFit: A quale is a philosophical term for a quality or property considered independently.

clue.text: Upmarket resort, rooms in ——? Torremolinos is wrong

indicators.note: wrong means mistaken, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: these letters plus the answer make up the anagram

explanation.surface: A travel agent mixes up two Iberian resorts when booking rooms.
explanation.walkthrough: The blank stands for the answer: 'rooms in' plus the answer is an anagram of TORREMOLINOS IS, the clue saying such a mix-up is wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Estoril is a fashionable seaside resort on the Portuguese Riviera near Lisbon.

clue.text: After workout, short, old uncle goes for a wine

indicators.note: After places the word for short behind the workout letters

parts.note: PE is physical education
terse means brief or short
eme is an archaic word for uncle

explanation.surface: After a gym session, an elderly uncle swaps his drink for wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter-see-me is an old English corruption of Pedro Ximénez, a sweet Spanish wine.
